transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doc. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. So, uh, I guess the main thing, the reason I finally made the appointment—which, by the way, my wife has been on my case about for months, probably since right around Thanksgiving when we had that whole blowout about the garage, but anyway—what really brought me in is that people just keep saying I'm not listening to them. 

It's not that I don't want to listen, you know? I work at the manufacturing plant, on the production floor, and sure, it gets loud out there, but even when it's quiet, it happens. Like, my supervisor will pull me aside, look me dead in the eye, and start explaining a shift change or a new safety protocol or something. And he'll be talking straight to me, right? Just me and him. But then, maybe a minute later, I suddenly realize my brain was just... I don't even know where it went. I realize I only caught maybe half of what he said, if that. And then I have to stand there looking like an idiot and ask him to say the whole thing all over again. He gets pretty ticked off about it.

And it's not just him, it's my wife, too. She'll be sitting right across the kitchen table from me, talking about her day or telling me about the bills, and I swear I'm looking right at her, but then she stops and waits for me to answer, and I have absolutely no idea what she just said. It's causing a lot of friction, you know? Because they think I don't care or I'm ignoring them on purpose, but I'm really not, I just... I just miss half of it and I don't know why.

When you're in a quiet place with no distractions—like at home in the evening—and someone is talking to you one-on-one, do you still have trouble following what they're saying, or does that mainly happen when there's background noise or other things going on around you?

Yeah, no, that's exactly it, it definitely happens when it's completely quiet, too. Like I was saying about my wife at the kitchen table. That's usually at night, right? The kids are in their rooms, the TV is off, it's just the hum of the refrigerator. It's literally as quiet as it gets in our house. And she'll be sitting right there, maybe three feet away from me. No radio, no nothing. And she'll be talking about, I don't know, her sister's upcoming visit, or maybe going over the electric bill because it was high last month, and I'm looking right at her. I'm making eye contact, nodding, doing the whole thing. 

But then... it's like a radio station losing its signal. One second I hear her saying "the due date is on the 15th," and then my brain is just... gone. I'm looking at her mouth moving, but I'm not actually hearing the words anymore. And then she stops, and I realize I've missed a solid minute of what she said. Like I mentioned, I only caught maybe half of it, if that. And I have to sit there and say, "Honey, I'm sorry, can you say that all again?" And man, she hates that. She really does. 

It's exactly the same deal with my supervisor. Even if he takes me into the little glass office on the production floor where it's soundproofed and quiet, it still happens. It's not the background noise, Doc. It's just... like I said, the whole reason I'm here is because people keep saying I'm not listening to them. They'll be talking straight to me, dead in the quiet, one-on-one, and a minute later I'm asking them to say it again because I only caught half of it. It's incredibly frustrating because I am trying, I really am, but the words just slip right past me.

When you're having one of these moments where you lose track of what someone is saying, does it happen right from the start of the conversation, or does it usually happen after they've been talking for a little while—like after a minute or two as you mentioned?

Yeah, no, it’s definitely not right at the very start. Like I was saying before, it’s usually after they've been going for a little bit. When my supervisor—Dave, his name is Dave, he's been there about five years longer than me—when Dave first walks up, I’m completely dialed in. I hear him say, "Hey, we need to talk about the line," and I’m right there with him. I say, "Sure thing, Dave, what’s up?" I hear the first few sentences perfectly fine. I’m nodding, I'm making eye contact. 

But then, yeah, exactly like I said earlier, it’s maybe a minute or so into it. He's still talking straight to me, and suddenly I just snap back to reality and realize my brain completely checked out. I'm still standing there, my body is there, but my mind just went on vacation. And that’s the whole reason I’m here, because people keep telling me I’m not listening, but I *am* listening at first! It's just that a minute goes by, and I suddenly realize I only caught half of what they said. 

Same thing with my wife. She'll sit down, she'll start talking about her sister, and I hear the beginning part. I know we're talking about her sister. But then she keeps talking, and a minute later, I'm just watching her lips move. It's like my tank only holds about sixty seconds' worth of gas for listening, and then it's empty. And then I have to do the walk of shame and ask them to say it all over again, which makes them think I wasn't paying attention from the jump, even though I was. It's just that delay, you know? I catch the start, and then a minute later I'm totally lost and asking them to repeat themselves.

Outside of conversations with people, do you have trouble concentrating or staying focused on other things—like reading a book, watching TV, working on a task at your job, or doing anything that requires you to pay attention for more than a few minutes?

No, see, that is the weird part about all this. It is really just the talking. If I am doing something else, I am completely fine. Take my job, for instance. I am on the floor running the stamping press, which is this massive piece of machinery, and you really have to be on your toes. You have the sheet metal coming in, you have to watch the alignment, check the pressure gauges, make sure the scrap conveyor at the back is not jamming up. And I can do that all day long. My shift is eight hours, sometimes ten if we are pulling overtime, which we have been lately because of all the supply chain stuff backing up, and I do not lose focus on that machine for a single second. If you zone out there, you could seriously get hurt, or you ruin a whole batch of expensive parts and Dave gets on your case again. So no, I am totally locked in when I am actually working on a task. 

And TV is the exact same way. I am totally fine there. Like on Sundays, they run these marathons of that show where they restore old muscle cars. I do not know if you have seen it, but they take these total rust buckets, like an old 69 Charger or something, and they completely tear them down to the bare frame, sandblast them, rebuild the carburetors, do all the custom upholstery, the whole nine yards. I can sit in my recliner and watch three or four hours of that straight, no problem at all. I do not miss a single detail of how they fix those engines. My wife actually gets mad at me for that, too, because she will say I am too focused on the TV and not paying attention to her or the stuff we need to do around the house. Which I guess brings us right back to the whole talking thing, because she will try to talk to me while the show is on and I am just glued to the screen. 

As for reading, well, I do not really read books. I have just never been a big book guy since high school, I do not have the patience to sit with a novel. But I read the sports articles on my phone, or I will go down a huge rabbit hole reading about fishing gear or looking up specs for truck parts for an hour, and I do not lose my place or forget what I am reading at all. 

It really is just when people are actually standing there talking to me. I do not know why it is different, but if my hands are busy or I am watching a process happen, my brain stays right exactly where it is supposed to be. It is just the conversations that just slip right out of my head.

When you're sitting with your wife at the kitchen table and you suddenly realize you've missed what she said—in that moment, can you actually hear the sound of her voice still coming out, or does it feel like the words have completely stopped reaching your ears?

Well, yeah, I can still hear the actual sound. It's not like my ears turn off or I go deaf or anything. I hear the noise she's making, like the pitch of her voice and the rhythm of it, but... it's just noise. It's exactly like that old Charlie Brown cartoon, you know? Where the teacher is just going "wah wah wah wah." I hear the "wah wah," but it's not English anymore. The words just lose their meaning entirely. 

And honestly Doc, like I keep saying, this right here, this exact thing, is what brought me in to see you in the first place. Because people just keep saying I'm not listening to them, and it's driving me crazy, and it's driving them crazy too. My wife will be right there at the table, or Dave down at the plant, they'll be talking straight to my face, looking me dead in the eye, and the sound of their voice is definitely hitting my eardrums. But a minute later, I'll snap out of it, and I realize I only caught maybe half of what they were saying. If that. Half is probably being generous, to be honest with you. 

And then I'm stuck in that terrible position where the sound stops, and it's my turn to talk, and I have absolutely no idea what I'm supposed to say. So I have to stop them and ask them to say it all over again. And you can imagine how well that goes over. My wife gets that look on her face, like her jaw tightens up and she takes this deep breath through her nose, and Dave just shakes his head and sighs like I'm the biggest idiot on the floor. But I'm not doing it on purpose! The sound is there, the words just... they don't turn into sentences in my brain. They just bounce right off. So yeah, I hear her voice still coming out, but it doesn't do me a lick of good because the information is just gone, and I still end up having to beg her to repeat the whole darn thing anyway.
Do you ever hear ringing, buzzing, whistling, or any other sounds in your ears when nobody is talking to you—like when you're just sitting quietly by yourself?

No, no, nothing like that. Which, honestly, you'd probably expect I would, right? Given where I work and all. I mean, the stamping plant is incredibly loud. You've got these massive presses coming down with tons of force, metal clanging on metal, the scrap bins getting dumped, the air compressors hissing all day long. It is an absolute racket in there. 

But the company is super strict about safety gear—you know, OSHA regulations and all that—so management makes sure we always have to wear these little orange foam earplugs. You have to roll them up real tight between your fingers and stick them deep in there, and then they expand. Sometimes I even wear the big heavy earmuffs over them if I'm working the really heavy press, just to be safe. So my ears are actually pretty well protected from all the noise. 

So yeah, when I get home and the house is actually quiet—like if my wife is out running errands and the TV isn't on—it's just pure quiet. I don't hear any whistling or buzzing or, you know, sounding like there's a mosquito trapped in my ear or anything. I know a guy at the plant, this older guy named Jimmy who's been there since the eighties, and he says his ears ring like a fire alarm 24/7 from his days before they made everyone wear the plugs. But I guess I got lucky there. 

When I'm just sitting out in the garage by myself, maybe having a cold beer after a long ten-hour shift, it's completely silent. Well, I mean, obviously I can hear the neighbor's dog barking two houses down, or the chest freezer humming in the corner, but inside my own head? In my actual ears? No, no extra noises at all. Just regular old quiet. Which is a relief, honestly, because my brain is always going a mile a minute anyway with a hundred different thoughts, so if I had some kind of constant buzzing in my ears on top of all that, I think I'd go absolutely crazy. But no, to answer your question, no ringing at all.

When your wife is talking to you at the kitchen table and you suddenly realize you've lost track of what she said, if she stops and repeats the exact same thing she just said word-for-word, can you understand it perfectly fine the second time around, or do you still have trouble catching it?

Yeah, if she repeats it, I get it perfectly fine the second time. And I know I probably sound like a broken record here, Doc, but like I was saying before, this whole situation is exactly what brought me in to see you in the first place. Because people just keep saying I’m not listening to them, and it happens all the time. My wife will be sitting right there across the kitchen table from me, or my supervisor Dave will be standing right on the shop floor talking straight to me, and I'll be nodding along, but a minute later I realize I only caught maybe half of it. If that. 

So then I have to do this whole awkward dance where I stop them and I'm asking them to say it again. And when she does—when she takes that deep breath and repeats it word-for-word—yeah, I understand it perfectly. It’s like my brain finally decides to hit the record button. I’ll lean forward, stare right at her mouth, and just force myself to catch every single syllable. I can process the information just fine when I know I'm on thin ice and I really, really have to focus. 

But getting to that point is just exhausting, you know? Because I have to sit there and admit that the first time she said it, it just evaporated. And nobody wants to have to say everything twice, especially when she’s just trying to tell me about her day at work or she's going over the grocery list or reminding me about the gutters needing cleaning. So the second time around, yes, it comes through clear as a bell. It’s just that first time where the words go in one ear and out the other, and I end up looking like a jerk who doesn't care about what she has to say. And I do care! I really do. It's just so frustrating having to constantly ask people to rewind and play it back for me just so I can get the actual message.

When your wife is talking to you at the kitchen table and you're in that moment where her voice sounds like 'wah wah wah'—at that exact moment, if someone suddenly asked you to repeat back just the last few words she said, could you do it, or are those words already gone by then?

Man, if she did that... and honestly, she actually does do that sometimes. She will just stop dead in her tracks and ask me what she just said or ask if I am even listening to her. And if I had to repeat it right then? I would be dead in the water. The words are just gone. Poof. Vaporized. It is like my brain did not even hit the record button in the first place. I might have some vague echo of the noise she was making, but the actual words? No way. 

And I know I am beating a dead horse here, Doc, and I know I keep coming back to this exact same point, but I really cannot stress it enough because this is it. This is the whole reason I finally swallowed my pride and made the appointment to come in here. People just keep telling me I am not listening to them, over and over again. It is the story of my life lately. My wife will be talking straight to me, or my supervisor Dave at the plant will be giving me instructions right to my face, and I am standing there nodding my head like I am totally tracking with them. But then a minute goes by, and I suddenly snap to attention and realize I only caught maybe half of it. If that. 

So then I am stuck, right? I am standing there feeling like a complete idiot, and I have to ask them to say it all over again. Because if I do not ask them to repeat it, I am going to mess up whatever it is they wanted me to do, whether that is picking up the right thing from the hardware store or running the press the right way. But yeah, to answer your question, if someone stops me in that exact moment and wants me to repeat the last few words back to them, I absolutely cannot do it. They are already long gone, just completely wiped from my head before they even registered.

When your supervisor Dave is giving you instructions about the stamping press—like telling you to adjust the pressure to a specific number, say 150 PSI, or telling you his name or the name of a part—do you have the same problem where a minute later you can't remember what number he said or what he called it, or does that kind of information stick with you better than when he's explaining something more complicated?

Man, I know I keep saying the exact same thing over and over, and I'm sorry if I'm talking your ear off about it, but... no, the short answer is no, the specific stuff doesn't stick any better. Even if it's just a simple number like 150 PSI, or a new guy's name, or a part number, it all just falls right out of my head exactly the same way. 

And like I said—and I know I'm a broken record today, but I really can't emphasize it enough—this specific thing is exactly what brought me in here to see you. Because people just keep saying I’m not listening to them, and it doesn't seem to matter if it's a long, complicated explanation or just one single number. Dave will be standing right there by the stamping press, talking straight to me, and he'll say, "Hey, run this next batch of brackets at 150." And I'll nod, and say "You got it, Dave." But then I turn around, walk maybe five or ten steps over to the control panel, and... I just freeze. A minute later, I realize I only caught half of the conversation. Did he say 150? Was it 115? Was it 150 for *this* batch or the *next* batch? The actual number is just completely gone. 

And you can't just guess with these machines, you know? You punch in the wrong pressure and you could ruin a whole run of expensive parts or seriously damage the die, and then you're really in hot water with management. So then I have to do the walk of shame. I have to go track Dave down by the scrap bins or the loading dock or wherever he wandered off to, and I'm asking him to say it again. "Hey Dave, what was that pressure again?" And he gives me this look, you know? Like, 'I literally just told you this sixty seconds ago, are you dense?' 

It's the exact same story with my wife. She'll look straight at me at the kitchen table and say, "Pick up the dog food at 4:00," and a minute later I'm pulling out my phone to text her, asking her to say it again because I can't remember if she said 4:00 or 4:30. I just... I only ever seem to catch half of it, no matter how simple or short the instruction is. And then I have to ask them to repeat it, which makes me look careless or like I don't give a damn, and that's just not true. It's incredibly frustrating.

When you're at the kitchen table with your wife and her voice turns into 'wah wah wah'—in that exact moment when it's happening, if you looked at her lips while she was talking, could you tell if she was saying the word 'dog' versus the word 'cat' just by watching her mouth move, or does it all look like gibberish too?

Honestly, Doc? If I'm already in that zone where it's all just noise... no, I couldn't tell you if she said dog or cat or... or pickup truck. I could be staring right at her lips, right at her face across the table, and it's just... it's just movement. It doesn't translate into actual words in my head. 

And I know, I know I'm beating this drum to death today, and I apologize for bringing it back to the exact same thing *again*, but I just can't get over how much this is messing up my life right now. Because this exact disconnect is the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair. It's what brought me in here. People just keep getting so angry, saying I'm not listening to them. And you can see why they think that, right? Because my wife will be talking straight to me, looking me right in the eye, or my supervisor Dave will be doing the exact same thing down on the floor, and I'm looking right back at them! My eyes are open, I'm watching them speak. 

But then a minute passes, the conversation stops, and I realize I only caught maybe half of what they said. If I'm lucky. So then I'm stuck having to ask them to say it all over again, and they get mad because they think I'm just ignoring them on purpose or that I don't respect their time. But I'm not! I could literally be watching her mouth form the word 'dog' and the signal just gets cut before it ever actually reaches my brain to tell me what she's saying. So yeah, to answer your question, it's all just visual gibberish at that point, too. It doesn't matter if I'm looking at her or not, if my brain has checked out, the words just aren't coming through.

When your wife is talking and it sounds like 'wah wah wah' to you, if she suddenly switched from speaking in English to speaking in a completely different language—like Spanish or French—would you notice that change right away, or would it still just sound like the same 'wah wah wah' noise to you?

Honestly? I swear to God, Doc, she could suddenly start rattling off the evening news in fluent Spanish or... or French, or whatever, and I probably wouldn't even bat an eye. Not right away, anyway. Because when I'm in that space, when the 'wah wah wah' thing is happening, it's not like I'm processing the sounds as language anymore. It's just... noise. Like a fan running in the background, or the hum of the conveyor belts down at the plant. It's just a continuous drone. So yeah, she could switch languages entirely and it would still just be that same Charlie Brown teacher noise to me. 

And I know... look, I know I am completely monopolizing this conversation with the exact same point, and I promise I'm not trying to drive you crazy by repeating myself for the fourth time today, but I just... I really need you to understand that this specific disconnect is exactly what brought me in here. It's the whole reason I'm sitting across from you right now. Because people just keep getting so fed up with me, constantly saying I’m not listening to them. And it causes fights with my wife, and it's putting my job on the line with my supervisor, Dave. They will be standing right there, talking straight to me—looking me dead in the eyes—and I'm standing there like a dummy, nodding along. And then a minute later, the fog lifts or whatever, the conversation ends, and I suddenly realize I only caught maybe half of what they were saying. If I'm lucky. 

And then I have to do the absolute worst part, which is swallowing my pride and asking them to say it all over again. And they get that look on their face, that 'are you kidding me' look, because they think I just don't care enough to pay attention. It's just... it's exhausting, you know? Living like this is exhausting. But yeah, to get back to your question, Spanish, French, English... if my brain has already checked out and turned it into that 'wah wah' sound, it's all just the same flat noise to me. I wouldn't notice the difference at all.

When your wife repeats something to you the second time and you understand it perfectly—is it because you're paying better attention that time, or does it actually sound clearer to you, like the words are sharper or easier to make out?

I know, Doc, I know. I'm doing it again. I'm circling right back to the exact same thing, and I promise I'm not trying to be difficult, but... well, to answer your question, it's definitely the attention. It's not like her voice suddenly gets louder or the acoustics in our kitchen magically change, you know? The sound itself doesn't get physically sharper. She doesn't have a megaphone all of a sudden.

What happens is... when she has to repeat it, or when I realize I've lost the thread, this kind of panic sets in. It's like cold water to the face. My brain suddenly snaps to attention because I know I've messed up again. So the second time she says it, I am zeroing in on her like my life depends on it. I'm forcing every ounce of energy I have into catching the words, so my brain is actually receiving the signal instead of just letting it bounce off into the void. 

And man, I know I have hammered this point into the ground since I sat down in this chair, but this whole miserable cycle is exactly what brought me in here to see you. It's the core of the whole problem. Because my wife, or Dave down at the plant, they'll be standing right there, talking straight to me, and I honestly think I'm with them in the moment. But then a minute later, the dust settles, and I realize I only caught half of it. Again. So I have to tuck my tail between my legs and ask them to say it a second time. 

And because I understand it perfectly that second time—because the panic made me focus—they think I was just being lazy the first time. They just keep saying I'm not listening to them, like I'm doing it on purpose to disrespect them. And it kills me, it really does, because I *want* to hear them the first time. It's just that the first time around, the engine isn't catching, no matter how hard I try.
Has your hearing ever been tested by an audiologist or a doctor? And if so, what did they find?

You know, it's funny you ask that, because my wife actually brought that exact same thing up a couple of months ago. We were having one of those arguments right there in the kitchen after I completely missed whatever she was telling me about her sister coming over, and she just threw her hands up and yelled, "Are you going deaf? You need to get your ears checked!" But no, I haven't actually gone to an audiologist or a specialist or anything like that. I mean, they do those basic, run-of-the-mill physicals down at the plant every couple of years for the insurance, where they stick you in a room and make you listen to the little beeps through those cheap foam headphones just to make sure the stamping machines haven't blown out your eardrums. And I always pass that with flying colors. I can hear a pin drop in the breakroom. I can hear a forklift backing up three aisles over. 

So I know for a fact it's not my ears. The hardware works fine, you know? It's the... I guess it's the software. Which—and look, I know I'm doing it again, I know I am sounding like an absolute broken record today, and I really am sorry for dragging us right back into the exact same mud puddle—but that is exactly why I'm sitting here talking to you. Because if it was just my hearing, if my ears were just shot from working on the production floor, I'd go get hearing aids and be done with it! Problem solved. 

But it's not that simple. Because people just keep getting so angry with me, constantly saying I'm not listening. Dave, my supervisor, he even made a crack about me needing to get my hearing checked just last week, and it really rubbed me the wrong way because I *can* hear him. I'm standing right there, looking at him, and the sound is definitely going into my ears. But then a minute later, the conversation ends, and I realize I only caught maybe half of what he actually meant. If I'm lucky. And then I'm stuck having to ask him to repeat the instructions, and he gets that annoyed look, thinking I'm just blowing him off. It's ruining my life, Doc. So, no, I haven't had any official hearing tests with a doctor, because I know my ears are fine. It's whatever is happening between my ears that's the problem.

When you're listening to music or hearing sounds that aren't words—like a song on the radio, or someone playing an instrument—do you have the same problem where after a minute or so the sound becomes like 'wah wah wah' and you lose track of it, or does that only happen when people are actually talking to you?

Music? No, music is totally different. Like, we have this beat-up radio down at the plant, usually tuned to some classic rock station or whatever, just playing over the noise of the machines while we're on the line. Or even when I'm just driving my truck home after a long shift. If a song is on, I might zone out during a guitar solo or something, sure, but it doesn't warp into that weird 'wah wah' noise. It just sort of... washes over me, you know? It doesn't matter if I miss a lyric because there's no pressure. The radio doesn't care if I'm paying attention. 

It only really happens when it's actual people talking to me. Which—and I know, Doc, I swear I know I am literally saying the exact same thing for the fifth time today, and you're probably thinking I'm physically incapable of talking about anything else—but I just can't stress it enough. It's the whole reason I finally picked up the phone and made this appointment. What brought me in here is that people just keep saying I’m not listening to them. It's always the same nightmare... my supervisor Dave, or my wife, they will be standing right there, talking straight to me, and I'm looking right back at them. And then a minute later, it's like a record scratch, and I realize I only caught half of it. If that. And then I have to swallow my pride and ask them to say it all over again. 

So yeah, to answer your question, it's not music or instruments or anything like that. It's strictly a conversation thing. It's just people.

When your wife is talking to you and it sounds like 'wah wah wah,' if she's saying a sentence like 'The dog is brown,' could you at least pick out individual words you recognize—like hearing the word 'dog' or 'brown'—or is it so scrambled that you can't make out any individual words at all?

Yeah, no, it's not completely... it's not like she's speaking Russian or something. I can definitely pick out individual words. If she says 'the dog is brown,' I'll probably catch 'dog.' Maybe 'brown.' But it's like... it's like Swiss cheese, you know? I get the pieces, but there are massive holes in between. I might hear 'dog' and then my brain just sort of stalls out for a split second, maybe thinking about if the dog needs to go out or if we're out of kibble, and by the time I tune back into her voice, the sentence is over and she's on to the next thing. So I have these fragments, just random words, but they don't connect into a full instruction or a full story. 

And I swear, Doc, I know I am beating this dead horse until it's absolute dust, and I know I've said this exact same thing to you like six times already today, but I just... I can't let it go because it's the entire reason I'm here. This is exactly what brought me in. It's just that people keep saying I'm not listening to them. It's always the same thing—my supervisor Dave, or my wife, they will be standing right in front of me, talking straight to me, and I'm looking right back at them, trying so hard to follow along. But then a minute later, the dust settles and I realize I only caught half of it. Just those little Swiss cheese pieces. And then I have to do the walk of shame and ask them to say it all over again. 

So yeah, I hear the words. I'll hear 'car' and 'Tuesday' and 'mechanic', but I won't have any earthly idea what actually needs to happen with the car on Tuesday. It's not that I don't hear any words at all, it's just that I never catch enough of them the first time around to actually know what's going on.

When your wife repeats something and you understand it perfectly the second time—if she then asked you to repeat back to her what she just said, word-for-word, could you do that accurately, or would you still struggle to hold onto the exact words?

Word for word? Man, I honestly don't know. I've never really tried to parrot her back exactly like that. I mean, usually when she has to say it the second time, she slows way down, you know? Like she's talking to a little kid. She'll say something like, take out the blue recycling bin, and at that point, I'm just so incredibly relieved that I finally caught the actual meaning of what she wants that I'm definitely not sitting there trying to memorize her exact sentence structure. I'm just thinking, okay, blue bin, got it, let me just go do it right now before I lose it again. 

Because by that second time around, there's always this heavy tension in the air. You can just feel it. She usually has her hands on her hips, she's giving me that specific look she gets, and my brain is just racing a mile a minute, just jumping all over the place trying to figure out how to fix the situation so she stops being mad at me. So if she suddenly stopped right then and there and demanded that I repeat exactly what she just said, every single word, I would probably just freeze up. I would know what she meant, like I'd know I need to pick up her sister at four o'clock, but did she say go get Sarah or did she say pick up my sister? I couldn't tell you. I just get the gist of it the second time around.
